power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) and a significant contributor to global hospitalizations for respiratory illness in infants and children. 1, 2 In 2023, two RSV preventive products were approved for use in the United States: a maternal vaccine to be administered during weeks 32 through 36 weeks of gestation, 3 and nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody administered to infants. 4 Nirsevimab was also approved for certain children up to 19 months of age entering their second RSV season who remain vulnerable to severe RSV disease. 4, 5 As of August 2026, children considered at increased risk of severe disease and recommended to receive nirsevimab in the second season in the U.S. included children of American Indian or Alaskan Native (AI/AN) descent and children with chronic lung disease of prematurity (CLD) requiring medical support in the six months before the RSV season, severe immunocompromise, or cystic fibrosis with manifestations of severe lung disease or weight-for-length <10 th percentile (Table 1). 4 The second season eligibility criteria were chosen based on previously identified conditions that were eligibility criteria to receive palivizumab, a short-acting monoclonal antibody that has since been discontinued in the U.S., and additional evidence indicating severe outcomes among children of AI/AN descent. 4, 6, 7 Nirsevimab effectiveness against severe RSV-related outcomes has been demonstrated in infants. 1, 8, 9 The population of children eligible to receive nirsevimab in their second season was small during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 RSV seasons, with eligible criteria impacting approximately 2%-4% of U.S. children 10, 11 As a result, there are few data assessing the effectiveness of nirsevimab in preventing severe RSV disease among high-risk U.S. children in their second RSV season.

text.text: Using data from the Overcoming RSV network, we our objective was to estimate the effectiveness of second season nirsevimab immunization against RSV-associated hospitalizations among children aged 8-23 months experiencing their second RSV season at U.S. pediatric hospitals.

The Overcoming RSV network, an extension of the Overcoming COVID-19 network, conducts RSV surveillance in 26 pediatric hospitals in 24 states. 8, 15 we used a casecontrol study with a test-negative design to assess nirsevimab effectiveness among children with conditions that conferred high risk for severe RSV and were 8-23 months of age in their second RSV season.

text.text: Hospitalizations were limited to those occurring during RSV season, from November 1, 2024-April 15, 2025, or September 15, 2025-April 15, 2026.
RSV test-positive case-patients were hospitalized for laboratory-confirmed RSVassociated symptoms or signs.

RSV test-negative control-patients were hospitalized with RSV-like respiratory symptoms or signs (i.e., cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, retractions, apnea, use of new or elevated oxygen support, or new pulmonary findings on chest imaging consistent with pneumonia) but tested negative for RSV ≤1 day before or during hospitalization.
Case-and control-patients were matched by site of enrollment, age category (8-15 months, 16-23 months), and hospital admission date (+/-2 months).
Up to two control-patients were identified per case-patient.
Case and control symptom onset for the current respiratory illness had to have begun within 14 days of hospitalization.

This activity was reviewed by CDC, deemed not research, and was conducted consistent with applicable federal law and CDC policy (See e.g., 45 C.F.R. part 46, 21 C.F.R. part 56; 42 U.S.C. §241(d); 5 U.S.C. §552a; 44 U.S.C. §3501 et seq.).

text.text: Demographic characteristics and clinical illness information were obtained through caregiver interview and medical record abstraction.
Information about second season nirsevimab-eligible and other preexisting health conditions was obtained through medical record abstraction.
Information about gestational age at delivery was collected for infants <12 months of age at admission.

text.text: Nirsevimab receipt was defined as having received one dose ≥7 days before symptom onset and after the end of the child's first RSV season.

Receipt was considered verified if documentation of a nirsevimab dose was confirmed in the child's medical record or the state's immunization information system, or if plausible receipt of nirsevimab was indicated in the caregiver interview and an exact or approximate date of receipt was provided.

Patients were not eligible for inclusion if nirsevimab receipt occurred within 7 days of symptom onset or during hospitalization, if symptom onset began more than 14 days before hospital admission, if nirsevimab receipt was not verified or did not have plausible caregiver-report, if the incorrect nirsevimab dose was received, if sites could not access the child's medical record or immunization information system record, if the patient did not have an RSV test result, or if they did not have a nirsevimab eligible condition.

We compared demographic and clinical characteristics between case-and controlpatients and patients who did and did not receive second season nirsevimab using chisquared, Fisher's exact, or Kruskal-Wallis tests.

We calculated effectiveness of second season nirsevimab against RSV-associated hospitalization using logistic regression, comparing the odds of nirsevimab receipt among case-and control-patients; effectiveness was calculated as 100%×(1-adjusted odds ratio).

Models were adjusted for age (in months), census region (Northeast, South, Midwest, and West), sex, month/year of hospitalization, and presence of a medical condition other than one conferring nirsevimab eligibility; site was included as a random effect.
Sites attempted to match control-patients to case-patients on age group and date of admission (+/-two months) in a two-to-one ratio.
However, because matching was unsuccessful for some cases, an unmatched complete case analysis was conducted as the primary model to assess nirsevimab effectiveness.
For all patients, we also assessed effectiveness of nirsevimab received in the 8-59 days before symptom onset, or ≥60 days before symptom onset.
A matched analysis, restricting to informative matched groups of case-and control-patients was conducted as a sensitivity analysis.

As an additional set of sensitivity analyses, we excluded case-and control-patients who tested positive for influenza or SARS-CoV-2, and evaluated effectiveness overall, by time since symptom onset, and in a matched analysis.
For all statistical analyses, pvalues <0.05 were considered statistically significant.

In the main analysis using unmatched data, overall adjusted estimated nirsevimab effectiveness against second-season RSV hospitalization was 78.1% (95% CI, 55.2%-89.3%) (Figure).

Point estimates of adjusted nirsevimab effectiveness were higher among patients that received nirsevimab 8-59 days prior to hospitalization (88.5% [95% CI, 63.4%-96.4%]) than among patients that received nirsevimab 60-178 days prior to hospitalization (69.8% [32.1%-86.5%]), although confidence intervals overlapped.
In the sensitivity analysis including only matched case-and control-patients, estimated adjusted nirsevimab effectiveness was 76.1% (95% CI, 41.8%-90.2%).

The conditions conferring second season nirsevimab eligibility in these two seasons in the U.S. are rare, making it difficult to assess nirsevimab effectiveness because of small sample size. 10 The second-season nirsevimab effectiveness observed in the current analysis of the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 seasons is similar to that observed for infants in their first RSV season in other populations.

All infants are recommended to be protected by either maternal RSV vaccination or receipt of monoclonal RSV antibody to prevent severe RSV during their first RSV season.

Residual immunity from products used in the first RSV season is not well established for the second season and is unlikely to be meaningful. 18 At least four studies have examined whether nirsevimab received in the first season is protective in the second season, with two studies reporting reduction in risk of RSV-related LRTI hospitalizations in the second season. text.text: In our analysis, approximately half of case-and control-patients had received nirsevimab in the first season, so this was unlikely to be an important factor influencing second season protection.

We observed in our network that RSV-positive children who received nirsevimab in their second season were more likely to have additional underlying health conditions than those RSV-positive children who did not receive second season nirsevimab.
These additional comorbidities may have contributed to the need for hospitalization in some children.

In addition, although patients were not tested systematically, coinfections with additional respiratory viral and bacterial pathogens were present among more than a quarter (28.6%) of the subset of nirsevimab-recipient case-patients tested.
These estimates among children 8 through 23 months represent effectiveness estimated among those children experiencing RSV circulation during the first three years of U.S. nirsevimab administration.

During the 2023-2024 RSV season, nirsevimab coverage among infants <8 months was 18.5,% 23 and increased to 44.7% in the 2024-2025 season. [24] [25] [26] Changes in the underlying epidemiology and burden of RSV may occur due to increased coverage of maternal RSV vaccination and nirsevimab use during the first RSV season.

text.text: Understanding how second season nirsevimab effectiveness may change when large proportions of the population are protected in the first season by RSV preventive products before entering their second season, and when nirsevimab coverage is higher among those in their second season, will be important.
This study has several strengths.
This is one of the first U.S. studies able to estimate second season nirsevimab effectiveness in this select population of children with conditions that place them at high-risk of severe RSV.

It used data from a large, heterogeneous population contributed by 26 U.S. hospitals, with enrollment using detailed medical record review and abstraction to identify nirsevimab-eligible conditions, and verification of nirsevimab receipt in order to reduce misclassification.

Further, using a strict clinical definition based on respiratory symptoms and signs for case-and control-patients, the test-negative design allowed control-patient selection from the same source population as the case-patients, reducing issues of confounding and selection bias. 27, 28 Because the conditions making a child eligible for nirsevimab receipt are rare in the population, 10 conducting a randomized clinical trial of second season nirsevimab to evaluate its efficacy would be infeasible due to difficulty recruiting sufficient numbers of eligible patients. 29 However, this study is subject to several limitations.

text.text: First, despite having data from two RSV seasons in this surveillance system, there were still relatively small numbers of case-and control-patients eligible to receive nirsevimab during their second RSV season.
Those patients enrolled in this analysis were predominantly eligible because they had chronic lung disease of prematurity.
It was not possible to assess effectiveness by specific underlying conditions conferring eligibility or to conduct subgroup analyses.

Second, clinical RSV testing was used to identify case-and controlpatients, but systematic testing for coinfections with respiratory pathogens was not conducted; therefore, we could not assess the impact of other pathogens on these results.

Third, because this was an observational test-negative study, it is subject to potential residual confounding; however, the results from the matched analysis were similar to the complete case analysis, providing some reassurance.

Fourth, this analysis was restricted to those eligible to receive nirsevimab during their second RSV season as of the time of study enrollment during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 RSV seasons, 6, 30 and effectiveness among other children potentially at high risk of severe RSV was not assessed.

text.text: In this case-control study using a test-negative design during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 RSV seasons, these data provide real world evidence that receipt of nirsevimab provided protection against RSV-associated hospitalizations for high-risk nirsevimabeligible children in their second RSV season.
